tagline.text: A sacred peak in Bakun and its stairway to the sky

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Day hike or 2 days and 1 night

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,150–4,000 (per person, 3 days and 2 nights by public transport from Baguio)

children.text: Mount Kabunian rises 1,789 m above the town of Bakun in Benguet. The Kankanaey regard it as a sacred mountain, the home of the sky god Apo Kabunian. It is known for its steep concrete staircase, the Stairway to Heaven, its suspension bridges and its sea-of-clouds views.
Mount Kabunian stands in the town of Bakun, Benguet, in the central Cordillera of northern Luzon, and its summit is
1,789 m above sea level
. Together with nearby Mount Tenglawan (1,943 m) and Mount Lubo (2,087 m) it forms the "Bakun Trio," and it is the best known of the three. The trailhead is in Bakun Poblacion (about
above sea level), and the climb to the summit gains more than 1,000 m.

The mountain is named after Apo Kabunian, the supreme deity of the Kankanaey people (a belief of the northern Kankanaey and others; his standing is said to differ somewhat between groups). Kabunian lives in the sky and gives bountiful harvests and protection, but is said to punish anyone who defiles his home with illness or curses. For this reason the mountain has long been a pilgrimage site where ancestors left offerings, and fenced burial sites with old wooden coffins still lie along the ridges and cliffs. Touching the coffins or photographing them up close is not allowed, so please keep this in mind before you hike.

The trail is a so-called "reverse hike." You descend toward the river right after the start, cross the first suspension bridge, and from there climb all the way to the summit. Along the way you pass forest paths, farm fields, three suspension bridges and the highlight of the hike, the steep staircase called the Stairway to Heaven (Takdag Camsit). The staircase is said to follow an old trade route linking the Cordillera interior with the Ilocos region (toward Kayapa and Tagudin in Ilocos Sur).
The route is about
10 km

round trip with roughly 1,030 m of cumulative elevation gain, rated 5/9 (trail class 2). It looks short, but there is little shade and the staircase section is punishing, so it is not recommended for first-time hikers. In return, the ridge and sea of clouds seen from the summit, and the quiet atmosphere of the village below, repay the preparation. The route up divides roughly into three parts: the first part, which goes down to the river and then climbs through forest on the far side; the middle part, which passes the rest shelter and continues up the staircase; and the final part, which follows the ridge from the junction to the summit. The descent uses the same trail, so allow for the fact that you must climb back up to the village at the very end, when your legs are tired.
This is the steep concrete staircase called Takdag Camsit. One side drops away, so you climb holding the ropes and railings, and it usually takes
1–1.5 hours
. Jump shots are not allowed here.
Suspension bridges cross the river at about
and
above sea level, one after another. They span the river, so hold the railing while you cross.

blocks.title: Burial sites on a sacred mountain

children.text: Old wooden coffins rest inside fenced enclosures on the cliffs and beside the trail. The fences protect them from animals such as goats, and visitors must not touch the coffins or photograph them up close.
The trailhead village of Poblacion has a tourism office (just outside Bakun National High School) and simple lodging. There is a
curfew, so the day ends early.
Hikers report that Smart, TNT and Globe data work at the summit. In the village, on the other hand, the signal is weak and GCash and Maya may not work, so bring cash.
Takdag Camsit is said to take its name from the story of a trader named Camsit, who died on this path when a boar he was trading dragged him down. "Takdag" means "fell" in Kankanaey.

This timetable is an example based on a November 2026 trip report. The ascent usually takes
4–5 hours
and the descent
3–4 hours

Climb by the same route as the day hike and camp on the summit ridge. Camping costs ₱150 per person, and an overnight guide is charged separately.
Campfires are not allowed. Carry out all your trash.
Watch the sunrise and sea of clouds, eat breakfast and head down.

The return bus is also reported to run once a day in the morning, so commuters using public transport may need to spend another night in Poblacion. There are reports that after the August landslides the Ampusongan section of the road is passable only by light vehicles, so check the latest road conditions.
Chartering a Monster Jeep from KM 5 reportedly costs about
per vehicle.
Group van tours from Manila cost
per person for a day hike and about
for an overnight trip. Many packages include transport, a guide and registration fees.
The best months for hiking are the dry season, November to May, and the skies are clearest from February to April. Early mornings are cool and clear, but by about
the sun is strong, and the concrete steps feel much hotter than the air.
From June to October heavy rain makes the trail slippery, afternoon fog rolls in, and landslides sometimes hit the access roads. Holy Week, April 9 and May 1 are crowded holidays, so register early.

The best time of day is dawn. Early morning is cool for walking, and your chances of seeing the sea of clouds from the summit are higher. At midday, by contrast, there is almost no shade on the ridge and the staircase, and it is tiring. When you plan, set your start time so that you pass the staircase before noon.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Poblacion has no large hotels. Lodging in the former municipal building is reported at about

per person per night, and if you want to start early it is best to sleep in the village the night before. Lodging and guides are booked through the Facebook page of the Bakun Municipal Tourism Council.

The village has only small eateries and sari-sari stores, and there are no shops or trash bins on the trail. Bring trail food and trash bags, and carry plenty of cash in small bills. There is reportedly no ATM in the village.

We recommend shopping in Baguio the day before your hike. Baguio has plenty of places to buy trail food, water and gear such as gloves and trekking poles, which makes up for the difficulty of finding anything you lack in Bakun. Group tours that travel from Manila in one go arrange lodging, meals and a guide for you, which is convenient for first-timers.
Reservations are required. Walk-ins are not accepted, and it is safest to apply to the tourism council at least
2 weeks
ahead (older guides said 3 days).
Bring a government-issued ID, and ask the tourism council in advance whether a medical certificate is required.
There is one guide for every 6 hikers. A group of seven needs two guides.
Bring 3–4 liters of water. Water sources along the trail can run low in the dry season, so treat them only as a backup.
Bring gloves, trekking poles and long pants. Gloves help when you grab rusty railings, and the concrete steps call for shoes with good grip.
Bring a headlamp for the early start, and wear a thin windbreaker at the summit.
Dress modestly and respect local customs concerning the mountain deity.
Guide overtime costs about ₱100 per hour after 6:00 PM, so start early if you expect to come down late.
You get a data signal at the summit, so tell your family when you expect to be back down.

After a grass fire on April 2, 2026, all climbs were suspended from April 3 (Executive Order No. 26, series of 2026), and we could not find a formal reopening notice. There is a record of a hike with a council-assigned guide in November, so be sure to check the latest status before you set out.
This is not a beginner's route. The staircase has drop-offs, and you need fitness and a head for heights.
Heat stroke is a risk. You need training on slopes and plenty of water.
Campfires are prohibited, and you must not touch the coffins or photograph them up close.
Poblacion has a
curfew.
Landslides on the access roads are frequent in the rainy season, so check road conditions.
You cannot climb without a guide, and registration is handled by the Bakun local government, not the DENR.
Another cultural site in the Cordillera, famous for its caves holding mummies. The route is different, so plan it as a separate trip.
A cool highland town in Benguet, worth considering alongside other trips in the mountains north of Baguio.
The city most hikers use as their base. It is a good place to shop the day before and set out from.
